name: Priya Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for doing this, Priya. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and everything you say here is confidential. Could you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I start with the pigs at seven, sixty-odd Saddlebacks on rotation through the woodland, then the hens. After that it's whatever the veg needs, which in November is mostly leeks, kale and clearing beds. Long Acre is a community farm, about forty hectares owned by a land trust, and around two hundred households pay a share each season and get a veg box. I also fly our little mapping drone and do the crop planning, which is my favourite nerdy bit.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you use technology day to day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Constantly, compared to most farmers. I ask an AI assistant every morning to pull together the weather, the soil sensor readings and the week's harvest list, and it writes the box newsletter drafts, which I then fix because it sounds too cheerful. I bought a second-hand drone with my own money, which is partly why our savings are only about two months right now. Lena, my girlfriend, is a nurse and thinks I talk to my phone more than to her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, honestly, that I'm a bit disappointed. I'd post something like, turns out the robots aren't coming to weed the carrots after all. At work I'd tell people we got some useful planning tools out of it, and that's not nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel like I bet on the wrong horse a little, spending on the drone and all the hours learning this stuff. But my actual job would be safe, and I'd still be the person on the farm who's quickest with the tools. That's not bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the AI tools for planning and records, and push to get the trust to pay for a soil sensor network, maybe two thousand for the whole farm. I'd build the savings back up to four months now the drone's paid for. And I'd keep pushing for a proper wage scale at the trust, because community farms are terrible at paying people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a little flatness. Like a show that got cancelled after one good episode.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said community farms are terrible at paying people. Tell me more.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everyone loves the idea of the farm and nobody wants to pay sixty a week for the veg box. So the trust runs on goodwill and volunteers, and the three of us who are paid get typical farm pay, which isn't much. AI or not, that's the thing I'd most like fixed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you have wanted AI to do on the farm, if it hadn't plateaued?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Weeding. Hand-weeding carrots in July is the worst job on earth, and there are small robots that can do it with a camera and a little blade. If AI stalls and those stay too expensive for us, I'll be on my knees in the carrot bed until I'm forty.

S0.say: I'd say I'm a bit disappointed and post something like, turns out the robots aren't coming to weed the carrots after all. At work I'd point out we still got useful planning tools.
S0.think: Privately I'd feel I bet on the wrong horse a little, with the drone and the hours learning. But my job would be safe and I'd still be the quickest person on the farm with the tools.
S0.do: Keeps using AI tools for planning and records and pushes the trust to spend about two thousand on soil sensors. Rebuilds savings from two months to four and keeps pushing for a proper wage scale at the trust.
S0.feel: Calm with some flatness, like a promising show cancelled early.
S0.quote: If AI stalls and those stay too expensive for us, I'll be on my knees in the carrot bed until I'm forty.
S0.fieldNote: Priya is the rare farmer who'd be let down by a plateau. Her disappointment is practical: she wants weeding robots to take the worst job off her. Even here, her real complaint is low pay on community farms, which she separates from the technology question.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is our chance to make farm work less brutal, if we do it right. I'd be the one sharing videos of weeding robots in the farmers' groups and saying, these should be shared between small farms, not just bought by the giants. And I'd say loudly that the workers need to be in the room when decisions get made.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think I'd do well out of it. I'm already the tech person at Long Acre, and if robots come in, someone has to run them, and it'll be me. My worry is more for the other two paid staff, especially Gwen, who loves the hand work and hates screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd write a proposal to the trust for a shared weeding robot between us and three other small farms nearby, maybe applying for a rural grant to cover half. I'd do an online course on farm robotics, probably evenings over the winter. And I'd start a small side thing setting up drone mapping for other farms, charging maybe a hundred a visit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly excited, if I'm honest. A little guilty about Gwen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a little guilty. What's that about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the thing I'm excited about might push Gwen out. She's been at Long Acre since it started, and her whole joy is hand-sowing and knowing every bed. I'd want to make sure the robot takes the carrot weeding, not her favourite jobs, but I'm not sure the trust would see it that way when money's tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Lena think of all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She rolls her eyes and says just don't automate the hospital. She sees all the tech failing at work, the computer systems that crash at shift change, so she's more sceptical than me. It's a good balance, actually; she keeps me honest.

S1.say: I'd say this is our chance to make farm work less brutal if we do it right, with robots shared between small farms rather than bought by the giants. I'd say workers need to be in the room for decisions.
S1.think: I think I'd do well out of it, since I'm already the tech person and someone has to run the robots. I worry more about my colleague Gwen, who loves the hand work and hates screens.
S1.do: Writes a proposal for a weeding robot shared with three nearby small farms, applying for a rural grant to cover half. Takes an evening online course in farm robotics over the winter and starts a side business doing drone mapping for other farms at about a hundred a visit.
S1.feel: Mostly excited, with some guilt about a colleague.
S1.quote: I'd want to make sure the robot takes the carrot weeding, not her favourite jobs, but I'm not sure the trust would see it that way when money's tight.
S1.fieldNote: Priya's adaptability and her progressive views fit together here: she'd bring in robots, but owned in common by small farms. Her guilt about Gwen is real and specific. Her partner's scepticism, grounded in hospital IT failures, acts as a brake she values.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs public control now, not in five years. Emergency rules on who owns the machines, and money for people while everything shifts. I'd be at the protests too, which I know sounds funny from the robot girl.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, two years is too fast even for me. If AGI can run the whole farm by 2028, including the robots and the planning, then my edge disappears, because I'm only ahead of other people, not ahead of the machine. And the trust would probably fold, because big automated farms would make veg so cheap that nobody pays for a box share.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move fast on the shared-robot idea while there's still a window, and try to make Long Acre the place that runs the machines for the area. I'd save harder, with no more gadgets, and I'd sign up to whatever campaign is pushing for public ownership. If the farm went under, I'd look for work setting up and running these systems for a council or a co-op, because that's where I'd rather be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Excited and scared at the same time, which is a strange mix to sleep on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the veg box scheme might fold. What would that mean for the people who pay into it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd probably be fine, honestly, with cheaper food in the shops. The people who'd lose are us, and the land would get sold to whoever has the robots. That's what keeps me up, picturing Long Acre fenced off and run by a company I've never heard of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You called yourself the robot girl. Is that how people see you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the village, yes, a bit. The older farmers call me that half as a joke. If it all happened in two years, I'm not sure it would stay a joke, because some of them would blame me just for liking it.

S2.say: I'd say we need public control now, with emergency rules on who owns the machines and money for people while things shift. I'd be at the protests too, even as the robot girl.
S2.think: Two years is too fast even for me, because I'm only ahead of other people, not of the machine. The community farm would probably fold if robot farms made vegetables very cheap.
S2.do: Moves quickly on the shared-robot plan to make the farm the area's machine hub, and stops buying gadgets to save harder. Joins campaigns for public ownership, and if the farm closes, looks for work running these systems for a council or co-op.
S2.feel: Anxious, a mix of excitement and fear that's hard to sleep on.
S2.quote: I'm only ahead of other people, not ahead of the machine.
S2.fieldNote: The fast scenario takes away Priya's advantage, and she sees that clearly. Her fear is less about her own job and more about the land being sold to a company. She also expects some blame from older farmers simply for having liked the technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to build something fair if we start this winter. I'd push for a network of community-owned farm robots, run through the land trusts, and I'd write to every council in the county. Online I'd be doing a lot of explaining, probably to people who don't want to hear it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years suits me. I'd be thirty-two, with a few years of running real robots behind me, and that's the kind of experience people would want. The bit I don't know is whether there's a job at the end, or just a few years of being useful before the machines run themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year: the shared robot, the robotics course, and the drone side business growing to maybe two days a month. By the third year I'd want a proper qualification, maybe a part-time degree in agricultural technology, which I'd pay for with the side income. I'd put money aside too, because I'm terrible at that, maybe getting to five months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a way I can use. It makes me want to get going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're terrible at saving. What gets in the way?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gadgets, mostly, if I'm honest. The drone, a better phone for the camera, a soil probe I used twice. Lena does the budget and she's started hiding the card when the agricultural show catalogue arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Gwen in this version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit her down, probably over tea at her kitchen table, and ask what she'd want to be doing at sixty. If it's still hands in soil, maybe that's teaching school groups or running the trust's seed library. I'd want her to choose, not have it chosen for her.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough to build something fair if we start this winter. I'd push for community-owned farm robots run through land trusts and write to every council in the county.
S3.think: Five years suits me, because at thirty-two I'd have real experience running robots. What I can't tell is whether there's a job at the end or just a few useful years before the machines run themselves.
S3.do: Gets the shared robot running, takes the robotics course and grows the drone business to about two days a month in the first year. Uses the side income to pay for a part-time degree in agricultural technology by year three, and tries to save five months of expenses.
S3.feel: Uneasy in a way she can use, which makes her want to get started.
S3.quote: Lena does the budget and she's started hiding the card when the agricultural show catalogue arrives.
S3.fieldNote: Priya has the most detailed plan for the five-year picture and sees it as suiting her career. She was frank about her weak saving habits and her partner's role in managing money. Her thoughts about her colleague turned to giving Gwen a real choice about her future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years, I'd say this is a once-in-a-century chance to redesign farming, so let's not hand it to the biggest companies by default. I'd want rural communities to own the machines and share the gains. I'd say that everywhere, and probably bore people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd feel pretty good about it. Ten years is a whole career's worth of learning, and I'd be thirty-seven, which isn't old. I'd want to end up designing how farms like ours work with these machines, rather than just driving them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on at Long Acre for a few years while doing the part-time degree, then move into a role, maybe with a co-op or a farm advice service, helping small farms set up and share robots. I'd help Gwen and the others plan as well. Lena and I might also look at moving closer to the city, where there'd be more of that work, but only once I had a job lined up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and quite hopeful. It's the one where I get to steer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in the ten-year picture that does worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That everyone relaxes and does nothing for eight years, and then it's the two-year version anyway, just later. I've watched the trust put off fixing the barn roof for four winters. People are good at waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned moving. How would you feel leaving Long Acre?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sad, really sad, because I know where every pig likes to wallow. But I'd still come back on weekends, and if the trust owned some of the machines because of work I did, it'd feel like I left something behind. That would make it okay.

S4.say: I'd say this is a once-in-a-century chance to redesign farming, so let's not hand it to the biggest companies by default. Rural communities should own the machines and share the gains.
S4.think: I'd feel pretty good, because ten years is a career's worth of learning and I'd only be thirty-seven. I'd want to end up designing how farms like ours work with the machines, not just driving them.
S4.do: Stays at the community farm for a few years while studying part-time, then moves into a co-op or farm advice role helping small farms set up and share robots. Helps colleagues plan and considers moving nearer the city with her partner once a job is lined up.
S4.feel: Calm and hopeful, because this is the version where she gets to steer.
S4.quote: I've watched the trust put off fixing the barn roof for four winters. People are good at waiting.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years makes Priya hopeful and ambitious; she wants to shape the change, not just survive it. Her one worry is that others will waste the time, which she illustrates with her farm's unfixed barn roof. Leaving the farm would hurt, but community ownership would make it feel worthwhile.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it wipes out the advantage I've worked for and there's no time to make things fair. What would help is public or community ownership of the machines, so the money stays local, and funded courses for people like Gwen who never wanted screens. And a decent income floor while it all settles.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: What the animals get out of it. A good robot could check every pig every hour, which no person does. A bad one could turn farms into factories. That choice is made by people, not by the AI.

headlineQuote: A good robot could check every pig every hour, which no person does. A bad one could turn farms into factories.
portrait: Priya Santos is 27 and works at Long Acre, a forty-hectare community farm owned by a land trust, looking after pigs and hens, growing vegetables and running the farm's drone and planning tools. She uses AI every day, lives with her girlfriend Lena, a nurse, and has only about two months saved after buying a drone. A plateau would mildly disappoint her, and steady change excites her, though she worries for a colleague who loves hand work. Only the two-year AGI picture makes her anxious, because it would erase her lead and could sink the community farm. With five or ten years she plans study, side income and community-owned robots, and feels she could help steer the change.
biggestWorry: AGI in two years, because it would wipe out the advantage she has built and leave no time to make the change fair.
whatWouldHelp: Public or community ownership of farm machines so the money stays local, funded courses for people who don't want screen work, and an income floor while things settle.
